prompt: Which statement best describes equality in the distribution of income?

options.label: A
options.text: An even distribution of income across people.

options.label: B
options.text: An efficient allocation of resources across uses.

options.label: C
options.text: A fair distribution accounting for differing needs.

options.label: D
options.text: An identical ranking of goods across consumers.

explanation: Equality concerns sameness or evenness of distribution. Equity is a normative idea about fairness and need not require identical incomes.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which statement best describes equity?

options.label: A
options.text: A requirement for identical income across people.

options.label: B
options.text: A judgement that an economic distribution is fair.

options.label: C
options.text: A condition for production at minimum average cost.

options.label: D
options.text: A measure of concentration in an income distribution.

explanation: Equity concerns fairness and therefore involves value judgements. Equal outcomes can be equitable in some contexts but equity does not mean equality by definition.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A government gives larger disability benefits to people with greater care needs. Which concept most directly justifies unequal payments?

options.label: A
options.text: Equality of outcome

options.label: B
options.text: Equity

options.label: C
options.text: Productive efficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Perfect competition

explanation: An equitable policy can deliberately treat people differently when their needs differ. Equal payments would be more equal but might be judged less fair.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Two households have equal disposable income, but one has much greater unavoidable medical costs. Why might equal income not imply equity?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal disposable income is impossible whenever households face different unavoidable costs, regardless of their earnings or taxes.

options.label: B
options.text: Their medical costs remove their economic choices.

options.label: C
options.text: Their needs and effective living standards may differ.

options.label: D
options.text: Their unavoidable costs establish their relative wealth.

explanation: Equity can take account of differing circumstances or needs. Identical money income may not provide an equally fair outcome where unavoidable costs differ.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which policy objective is most directly about equality rather than equity?

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing support for households with greater care needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing differences in disposable incomes.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing transfers in proportion to unavoidable housing costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing disparities in treatment for equally needy households.

explanation: Reducing income dispersion targets equality. Equity asks whether the resulting distribution is fair, which may depend on needs, contribution or other normative criteria.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country’s Gini coefficient falls. What can be inferred most directly?

options.label: A
options.text: The measured income distribution has become more equal.

options.label: B
options.text: The measured income distribution has become more equitable.

options.label: C
options.text: The measured level of absolute poverty has disappeared.

options.label: D
options.text: The measured level of productive efficiency has increased.

explanation: A lower Gini coefficient indicates greater equality of the measured distribution. Whether the change is more equitable is a normative judgement and cannot be inferred from the coefficient alone.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why is equity a normative concept?

options.label: A
options.text: Observed market prices alone establish which distribution is fair, without requiring any judgement about needs or contributions.

options.label: B
options.text: Fairness judgements follow directly from measured national output.

options.label: C
options.text: Fairness judgements depend only on observed production costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Fairness judgements depend on values as well as facts.

explanation: Economists can measure distributions, but deciding what distribution is fair requires ethical or value judgements.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which change increases equality but could be judged inequitable by some people?

options.label: A
options.text: Leaving every household’s disposable income unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Equalising incomes without accounting for need or contribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the incomes of the highest earners alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing transfers to households with the lowest incomes.

explanation: A redistribution can narrow income differences yet be considered unfair under some value systems. Equality and equity therefore need not move together.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: If everyone in an economy receives exactly the same money income, which statement must be true?

options.label: A
options.text: Income and needs are equally distributed.

options.label: B
options.text: Income is equal, but equity is not established.

options.label: C
options.text: Income and wealth are equally distributed.

options.label: D
options.text: Income is equal, so resource allocation is efficient.

explanation: Equal money incomes establish equality of income, but equity depends on judgements about needs, effort and circumstances. Wealth can also remain unequal.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government gives all children the same education grant even though some live in remote areas with higher schooling costs. Which criticism is based on equity?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal grants may provide unequal effective access to schooling.

options.label: B
options.text: Equal grants imply equal schooling costs across different locations.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal grants establish that every child has identical needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Equal grants imply that remote schools use fewer resources.

explanation: Treating unlike circumstances identically may be equal in a narrow sense but inequitable if the aim is fair opportunity.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which pair is correctly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: Equality: even distribution; equity: fair distribution.

options.label: B
options.text: Equality: fair distribution; equity: cost minimisation.

options.label: C
options.text: Equality: cost minimisation; equity: identical outcomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Equality: productive efficiency; equity: allocative efficiency.

explanation: Equality concerns how evenly outcomes are distributed. Equity is the broader normative concept of fairness.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: An economy becomes more unequal but the poorest households are substantially better off. What can be concluded about equity?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater inequality establishes that the outcome is less fair.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher poor-household incomes establish that the outcome is fairer.

options.label: C
options.text: A higher national income establishes that fairness is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Assessing fairness requires a judgement about the resulting distribution.

explanation: The facts describe changes in absolute living standards and inequality, but equity remains a value judgement. Different ethical criteria can lead to different conclusions.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A policy provides the same universal benefit to every adult. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal payments establish an equal income distribution.

options.label: B
options.text: Equal payments establish an equal wealth distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal payments do not establish equitable outcomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Equal payments remove all differences in needs.

explanation: Uniform payments can contribute to equality at the payment stage, but distributional effects depend on taxes used to finance the scheme and differences in need and income.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which is the clearest example of unequal treatment intended to promote equity?

options.label: A
options.text: Providing equal transfers to households with differing needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Charging equal taxes to households with differing incomes.

options.label: C
options.text: Setting equal wages for occupations with differing requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Providing larger transfers to households with lower incomes.

explanation: Targeted redistribution treats households differently because their circumstances differ. This can be justified on equity grounds even though the treatment is unequal.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is meant by economic efficiency in the context of equity and redistribution?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocating identical incomes regardless of household preferences.

options.label: B
options.text: Allocating universal benefits regardless of household resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Allocating scarce resources without avoidable welfare losses.

options.label: D
options.text: Allocating public funds regardless of opportunity costs.

explanation: Efficiency concerns how effectively scarce resources are used, while equity concerns fairness. Redistribution may improve equity but can affect incentives and resource allocation.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why can a more progressive income tax create an equity-efficiency trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater equality increases the return to additional work.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater equality increases the after-tax return to investment.

options.label: C
options.text: Redistribution may weaken work and investment incentives.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater equality removes the need to finance public spending.

explanation: Higher marginal tax rates can redistribute disposable income, but they may also alter behaviour and reduce the efficiency gains from additional work or investment.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which policy could improve both equity and efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Price support that encourages production of unwanted agricultural surpluses.

options.label: B
options.text: Targeted education support that relaxes poor households’ credit constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: A production subsidy that encourages waste in a protected monopoly.

options.label: D
options.text: Entry restrictions that prevent low-income workers entering skilled occupations.

explanation: If poor households under-invest in education because of credit constraints, targeted support can widen opportunity and raise human capital, potentially improving both fairness and productive capacity.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A redistribution policy reduces measured inequality but causes some high-skilled workers to leave the country. What is the most likely efficiency concern?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy may gain productive capacity as skilled workers leave.

options.label: B
options.text: The economy may raise labour productivity as skilled workers leave.

options.label: C
options.text: The economy may expand its tax base as skilled workers leave.

options.label: D
options.text: The economy may lose productive human capital and tax revenue.

explanation: Migration responses can reduce the tax base and productive capacity. This illustrates why distributional gains should be weighed against behavioural effects.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement best captures the relationship between equity and efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Every redistribution reduces efficiency, including policies that improve poor households’ health and employment opportunities.

options.label: B
options.text: They are identical under every possible redistribution policy.

options.label: C
options.text: They can conflict, but a policy can improve both.

options.label: D
options.text: They describe only judgements about fairness of distribution.

explanation: Redistribution can distort incentives, creating a trade-off, but policies that improve access to education, health or opportunity may raise both equity and efficiency.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government introduces a benefit that is withdrawn pound-for-pound as earned income rises. Why can this reduce efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Benefit withdrawal lowers the effective marginal tax rate.

options.label: B
options.text: Benefit withdrawal raises the effective marginal tax rate.

options.label: C
options.text: Benefit withdrawal lowers the marginal cost of employing workers.

options.label: D
options.text: Benefit withdrawal raises the marginal product of employing workers.

explanation: When benefit withdrawal offsets extra earnings, the net gain from work is small or zero. This can weaken labour-supply incentives and contribute to a poverty trap.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A redistribution policy raises the incomes of the poorest households and increases their access to preventive healthcare. How might this improve efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Better health may remove all differences in household incomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Health improvements can raise productivity and reduce treatment costs.

options.label: C
options.text: Better health may make healthcare resources freely available.

options.label: D
options.text: Better health may eliminate the opportunity cost of medical training.

explanation: Improved health can increase effective labour supply and productivity. Redistribution can therefore sometimes have efficiency benefits as well as equity benefits.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is the strongest efficiency criticism of a universal benefit paid to high-income and low-income households alike?

options.label: A
options.text: Unnecessary payments may displace spending or require distortionary taxes.

options.label: B
options.text: Universal benefits exclude low-income households from receiving public transfers.

options.label: C
options.text: Universal benefits require every recipient to stop earning employment income.

options.label: D
options.text: Financing universal benefits prevents any change in other public spending.

explanation: Universal schemes reduce exclusion and stigma but are fiscally expensive because many payments are not targeted at poverty reduction.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | 8.2.5 Policies towards equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which outcome is allocatively efficient but may still be judged inequitable?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal incomes with scarce resources wasted in production.

options.label: B
options.text: MSB equals MSC with income concentrated among few households.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal incomes with scarce resources allocated where MSB exceeds MSC.

options.label: D
options.text: Income concentrated among few households with output where MSC exceeds MSB.

explanation: Allocative efficiency concerns the use of resources, not the fairness of the resulting income distribution. An efficient market outcome can still be highly unequal.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A tax-funded transfer allows a low-income child to remain in education rather than leave school for work. Why might the long-run efficiency cost of redistribution be smaller than expected?

options.label: A
options.text: Additional schooling removes scarcity of current public funds.

options.label: B
options.text: Additional schooling may raise the child’s future productivity.

options.label: C
options.text: Additional schooling removes taxation’s effects on work incentives.

options.label: D
options.text: Additional schooling makes public funding a lump-sum tax.

explanation: Redistribution that finances productive investment can generate future benefits. Its net efficiency effect depends on both tax distortions and the productivity gains from the spending.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government wants to redistribute income with the smallest possible distortion to work incentives. Which design principle is most relevant?

options.label: A
options.text: Withdraw benefits rapidly over a narrow earned-income range.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove every benefit when a recipient starts employment.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase marginal tax rates sharply at each benefit threshold.

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid sharp benefit withdrawal over narrow earned-income ranges.

explanation: Large effective marginal tax rates reduce the net return to extra work. Smoother withdrawal can reduce the poverty-trap effect, although it may increase fiscal cost.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change is most likely to increase equality while reducing productive efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Targeted vaccinations that improve low-income workers’ health.

options.label: B
options.text: Redistribution that substantially reduces productive workers’ labour supply.

options.label: C
options.text: Targeted training that improves low-income workers’ skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Redistribution that removes poor households’ barriers to skilled employment.

explanation: The redistribution narrows income differences, but if the behavioural response substantially reduces output, productive efficiency can worsen.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why is there no universal economic rule for the optimal degree of redistribution?

options.label: A
options.text: Fairness follows directly from observed market prices.

options.label: B
options.text: Behavioural responses are identical under different taxes.

options.label: C
options.text: Fairness judgements and efficiency estimates both matter.

options.label: D
options.text: Equity follows solely from positive economic analysis.

explanation: The efficiency consequences can be studied empirically, but the weight placed on equality and fairness is normative. Different societies can rationally choose different points on the trade-off.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A policy increases equality of opportunity by subsidising access to vocational training. Which effect would most strengthen the case that it also improves efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Workers remain in occupations where their skills are underused.

options.label: B
options.text: Workers become less able to move between different occupations.

options.label: C
options.text: Firms experience increased shortages of appropriately trained workers.

options.label: D
options.text: Workers move into jobs where their productivity is higher.

explanation: If training improves occupational mobility and productivity, the policy can increase both access and the efficiency of labour allocation.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about a Pareto improvement and equity is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A Pareto improvement requires incomes to become equal.

options.label: B
options.text: A Pareto improvement requires the richest person’s loss.

options.label: C
options.text: A Pareto improvement requires transfers to poorer households.

options.label: D
options.text: A Pareto improvement can leave incomes highly unequal.

explanation: A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off, but it says nothing about how equal or fair the distribution is.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A progressive tax raises revenue for transfers but also finances better tax enforcement that reduces evasion. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: The net effects establish reduced equity and reduced efficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: The net effects depend on behavioural and administrative responses.

options.label: C
options.text: The net effects establish increased equity and reduced efficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: The net effects establish increased equity and increased efficiency.

explanation: Progressive taxation can distort behaviour, but improved enforcement can broaden the base and reduce unfair evasion. The overall effect needs evidence rather than a one-direction assumption.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.2 Difference between equity and efficiency | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: What is absolute poverty?

options.label: A
options.text: Insufficient resources to meet a defined basic-needs standard.

options.label: B
options.text: Income below a fixed share of national median income.

options.label: C
options.text: An uneven distribution of financial and non-financial wealth, irrespective of whether households can meet basic needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Income below the economy’s average income per person.

explanation: Absolute poverty is judged against a minimum standard or poverty line intended to reflect basic needs, rather than against the incomes of others in the same society.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is relative poverty?

options.label: A
options.text: Poverty measured relative to society’s prevailing living standards.

options.label: B
options.text: Poverty measured against a fixed real basic-needs basket.

options.label: C
options.text: Poverty measured by the share of workers without employment.

options.label: D
options.text: Poverty measured solely by financial asset ownership, without comparing income or living standards across households.

explanation: Relative poverty compares a household’s resources with those of the wider society, often using a proportion of median income.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Real incomes of the poorest households rise, but median income rises even faster. Which outcome is possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Absolute poverty rises while relative poverty rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Absolute poverty rises while relative poverty falls.

options.label: C
options.text: Absolute poverty falls while relative poverty falls.

options.label: D
options.text: Absolute poverty falls while relative poverty rises.

explanation: Higher real incomes can move households above an absolute poverty line, while a faster rise in the median can leave them further below a relative threshold.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A recession lowers the median income sharply while the incomes of the poorest households fall only slightly. What may happen to a relative poverty measure?

options.label: A
options.text: It may fall despite declining real incomes among poor households.

options.label: B
options.text: It must rise in proportion to the decline in national output.

options.label: C
options.text: It must fall in proportion to the decline in national output.

options.label: D
options.text: It may rise only if poor households’ real incomes increase.

explanation: Because the relative threshold is tied to typical income, a fall in the median can lower the poverty line. This can reduce measured relative poverty despite little or no improvement in living standards.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which policy would most directly reduce absolute poverty if successful?

options.label: A
options.text: Raising real incomes of households below the basic-needs line.

options.label: B
options.text: Raising real incomes of households above the basic-needs line.

options.label: C
options.text: Lowering the real income of the median household alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Lowering the real income of the highest earners alone.

explanation: Absolute poverty falls when households gain enough real resources to meet the specified minimum standard.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why does relative poverty tend to remain possible even in a high-income economy?

options.label: A
options.text: It depends on whether the real basic-needs basket is affordable.

options.label: B
options.text: It depends on income relative to society’s prevailing income level.

options.label: C
options.text: It depends on whether the economy has zero real GDP growth.

options.label: D
options.text: It depends on whether household wealth exceeds average national wealth.

explanation: A rich country can still have households far below the typical standard of living, so relative poverty can persist even when basic material needs are widely met.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country doubles every household’s real income with no change in the income distribution. What happens to relative poverty measured as a fixed percentage of median income?

options.label: A
options.text: The proportion below the threshold falls to zero.

options.label: B
options.text: The proportion below the threshold doubles.

options.label: C
options.text: The proportion below the threshold halves.

options.label: D
options.text: The proportion below the threshold stays unchanged.

explanation: Every income and the median double together, so each household’s income as a share of the median is unchanged. The proportion below the fixed percentage threshold is unchanged.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country doubles every household’s real income with no change in the distribution. What is most likely to happen to absolute poverty using a fixed real poverty line?

options.label: A
options.text: The proportion in absolute poverty necessarily stays unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: The proportion cannot rise and may fall.

options.label: C
options.text: The proportion in absolute poverty necessarily doubles.

options.label: D
options.text: The proportion becomes identical to relative poverty.

explanation: Doubling every real income cannot move anyone below a fixed real poverty line. Some households may cross above it, reducing absolute poverty; the headcount need not fall if no household crosses.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Relative poverty requires income below the basic-needs poverty line.

options.label: B
options.text: Absolute poverty requires income below a share of median income.

options.label: C
options.text: Relative poverty disappears once absolute poverty has been eliminated.

options.label: D
options.text: Relative poverty can persist above the basic-needs poverty line.

explanation: A household may meet basic needs yet still have income far below the typical standard of the society, so the two poverty concepts can classify it differently.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can an absolute poverty line require periodic adjustment?

options.label: A
options.text: Inflation changes the money needed to buy the basic-needs basket.

options.label: B
options.text: Inflation changes the real quantities contained in a fixed basket.

options.label: C
options.text: Inflation automatically raises every poor household’s real purchasing power.

options.label: D
options.text: Inflation automatically reduces every poor household’s real purchasing power.

explanation: If the line is intended to represent a constant real minimum, its nominal value needs to rise with the cost of the relevant basket.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government reports that no household is below its absolute poverty line. Which statement may still be true?

options.label: A
options.text: Income inequality and relative poverty must both disappear.

options.label: B
options.text: Income inequality and relative poverty can remain substantial.

options.label: C
options.text: Income inequality must disappear although relative poverty may remain.

options.label: D
options.text: Relative poverty must disappear although income inequality may remain.

explanation: Eliminating severe deprivation does not imply an equal or universally judged fair distribution. Relative poverty can remain because it is based on the social distribution.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which measure is most sensitive to a change in the median income even if a poor household’s own income is unchanged?

options.label: A
options.text: A poverty threshold fixed as a share of median income.

options.label: B
options.text: A basic-needs poverty threshold whose real purchasing power stays fixed despite changes in median income.

options.label: C
options.text: A household’s own income measured in current money units.

options.label: D
options.text: A household’s own wealth measured in current money units.

explanation: By construction, a relative threshold moves with the median. An absolute line can be fixed in real purchasing-power terms instead.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A household’s nominal income rises by 5% while the price of its basic-needs basket rises by 10%. What happens to its ability to escape absolute poverty, other things equal?

options.label: A
options.text: It improves because purchasing power over basic needs rises.

options.label: B
options.text: It is unchanged because nominal income and prices both rise.

options.label: C
options.text: It improves because the basic-needs poverty threshold falls.

options.label: D
options.text: It worsens because purchasing power over basic needs falls.

explanation: Absolute poverty depends on real command over basic goods and services. A 5% nominal income rise is insufficient to offset a 10% increase in the relevant cost of living.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: The median income rises from $20 000 to $25 000 and relative poverty is defined as below 60% of median income. What is the new relative poverty threshold?
explanation: The threshold is 0.60 × $25 000 = $15 000.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A household earns $14 000 after the median rises to $25 000. If relative poverty is below 60% of median income, how is the household classified?

options.label: A
options.text: Above the relative threshold of $12 000.

options.label: B
options.text: At the relative threshold of $14 000.

options.label: C
options.text: Below the relative threshold of $15 000.

options.label: D
options.text: Above the relative threshold of $15 000.

explanation: The threshold is $15 000. Since the household receives $14 000, it lies below the relative poverty line.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is a limitation of using only a national relative poverty line?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal incomes can buy different living standards when needs differ.

options.label: B
options.text: Income data cannot be collected for households in different regions.

options.label: C
options.text: The same national income threshold must place every household below it.

options.label: D
options.text: Relative poverty measures identify differences in firms’ average production costs.

prompt: What is the poverty trap?

options.label: A
options.text: Benefit payments remain unchanged as earned income increases.

options.label: B
options.text: Benefit payments increase faster than a household’s earned income.

options.label: C
options.text: Taxes and benefit withdrawal leave little extra disposable income.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher wages raise disposable income without any benefit withdrawal.

explanation: The poverty trap arises from high effective marginal tax rates created by the interaction of taxes and benefit withdrawal, weakening the financial incentive to earn more.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A worker earns an extra $100, pays $20 extra tax and loses $70 of means-tested benefit. By how much does disposable income rise?
explanation: The worker keeps $100 - $20 - $70 = $10. The 90% effective marginal deduction illustrates how a poverty trap can weaken work incentives.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is the effective marginal deduction rate if $90 of each additional $100 of earnings is lost through tax and benefit withdrawal?
explanation: The effective marginal deduction rate is the amount of extra earnings lost divided by extra earnings: 90/100 = 90%.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why are means-tested benefits more likely than universal benefits to contribute to a poverty trap?

options.label: A
options.text: Universal benefits are reduced as recipients earn additional income.

options.label: B
options.text: Universal benefits increase the tax rate on each additional dollar.

options.label: C
options.text: Means-tested benefits are withdrawn as recipients earn additional income.

options.label: D
options.text: Means-tested benefits increase without regard to recipients’ additional income.

explanation: Means testing improves targeting but withdrawal can reduce the financial gain from work. Universal benefits do not normally fall simply because earned income rises.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | 8.2.5 Policies towards equity and equality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which policy change is most likely to reduce a poverty trap?

options.label: A
options.text: Withdraw benefits immediately when earnings exceed a low threshold.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the tax on additional low earnings to 100%.

options.label: C
options.text: Withdraw means-tested benefits more gradually as earnings rise.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the whole benefit when a recipient enters employment.

explanation: A slower taper reduces the effective marginal tax rate, increasing the amount of extra earnings retained. The trade-off is that more households remain eligible, increasing fiscal cost.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A household receives $500 of benefit at zero earnings. The benefit falls by $0.60 for every $1 earned. Ignoring tax, how much benefit remains when earnings reach $400?

prompt: With a 60% benefit withdrawal rate and a 20% income tax on extra earnings, what is the combined effective marginal deduction rate?
explanation: For each extra dollar, $0.60 of benefit is lost and $0.20 of tax is paid. The household retains $0.20, so the effective marginal deduction rate is 80%.

prompt: What labour-market effect can result from a poverty trap?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Some individuals may reduce work because the net reward is small.

options.label: D
options.text: Some individuals may reduce work because their hourly wage rises.

reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.4 The poverty trap | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why does eliminating means testing entirely not necessarily solve the policy problem at low cost?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Universal payments eliminate the need to finance transfer expenditure.

options.label: C
options.text: Universal payments are automatically financed from higher recipients’ incomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Universal payments avoid withdrawal effects but cost more.

prompt: A person refuses a small pay rise because it would cause the loss of a large housing benefit. This is evidence of

prompt: Which policy is most likely to reduce relative poverty if financed progressively and set at a substantial level?

options.label: A
options.text: A transfer concentrated on households below the relative poverty line.

options.label: B
options.text: A tax concentrated on households below the relative poverty line.

options.label: C
options.text: A subsidy concentrated on households above the relative poverty line.

options.label: D
options.text: A transfer reduction concentrated on households below the relative poverty line.

explanation: Targeted transfers raise the incomes of households below the relative threshold, while progressive financing can reduce disposable incomes at the top, tending to narrow the distribution.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.5 Policies towards equity and equality | 8.2.3 Distinction between absolute poverty and relative poverty | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A universal benefit raises every household’s income by the same dollar amount. Why can it still reduce measured income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: The same addition is proportionately larger for high-income households.

options.label: B
options.text: The same addition is withdrawn as recipients’ earned incomes rise.

options.label: C
options.text: The same addition reduces the income of every low-income household.

options.label: D
options.text: The same addition is proportionately larger for low-income households.

explanation: An equal absolute payment represents a larger percentage increase in a small income than in a large one, tending to compress relative income differences before financing is considered.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.5 Policies towards equity and equality | universal benefits | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government compares universal and means-tested transfers with the same total transfer budget. Assume equal administration costs, full take-up, and a means test restricting eligibility to poor households. Which offers each poor recipient the larger payment?

options.label: A
options.text: Universal: the budget is shared across more recipients.

options.label: B
options.text: Universal: income tests increase the number of recipients.

options.label: C
options.text: Means-tested: the budget is shared across fewer recipients.

options.label: D
options.text: Means-tested: universal eligibility increases the number of recipients.

explanation: For a fixed budget, targeting fewer eligible households allows a larger transfer per recipient. The trade-off is more administration and possible withdrawal disincentives.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.5 Policies towards equity and equality | universal and means-tested benefits | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which factor is most important when judging whether a redistribution policy improves equity?

options.label: A
options.text: Gross payments without considering recipients’ other income or needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Fiscal costs without considering who receives the transfer payments.

options.label: C
options.text: Final gains and losses including both benefits and financing.

options.label: D
options.text: Eligibility rules without considering taxes used to fund payments.

explanation: Net incidence matters. A benefit that looks progressive can be offset by regressive financing, while a universal payment can be progressive after tax.
reference: 8.2 Equity and redistribution of income and wealth | 8.2.5 Policies towards equity and equality | 8.2.1 Difference between equity and equality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Why may cash transfers be preferred to in-kind benefits by some economists?

options.label: A
options.text: Recipients must spend cash only on government-selected products.

options.label: B
options.text: Recipients face no opportunity cost when spending the cash.

options.label: C
options.text: Recipients must give up their ability to compare available products.

options.label: D
options.text: Recipients can spend cash according to their own preferences.

explanation: Cash gives households flexibility, but in-kind provision may be preferred when governments are concerned about merit goods, information or how transfers are used.
